title: Howie Rose’s Iconic Career Is Going in the Books
subtitle: The beloved Mets announcer is the latest in a changing of the guard that has reshaped broadcasting booths for half of MLB’s franchises over the past decade.
contentHtml:
Perhaps uniquely among the major sports, baseball announcers forge a special relationship with fans who tune in for the game. For local broadcasters, they practically become honorary family members — granted, in a parasocial kind of way — because of their omnipresence, night-in and night-out, for six months (or more) each spring and summer. It is the privilege and responsibility everyone in the booth carries, and those who are particularly good at it can remain there long enough to narrate entire generations worth of memories.

Subscribe now

New York Mets radio voice Howie Rose is one of the best to ever get behind a mic, whether calling hockey — his reaction to Stephane Matteau’s winning goal in Game 7 of the East final stands among the most iconic calls in any sport, ever…

…or baseball, where he has been a fixture narrating games on television and/or radio in Queens for more than three decades.

Rose, who at age 72 this year scaled back to calling Mets home games only, tearfully signed off on what he thought might be his last game as a regular MLB announcer on Saturday, in the host squad’s 10-3 win over the rival Philadelphia Phillies. “Just know that I love you all,” Rose said after the game.

(While the Mets were set to finish their last 2026 homestand on Sunday, rain forecasts threatened the game and caused Rose’s farewell ceremony to be canceled. However, the game was played amidst the drizzle and Rose was there to call the action, receiving chants from the crowd and a hat-tip from the players during his final inning.)

Along with Mike Krukow of the San Francisco Giants and Rick Rizzs of the Seattle Mariners, Rose is one of three radio and/or TV broadcasters tenured 30+ years to leave their posts after this season. Meanwhile, last season saw Buck Martinez leave the Toronto Blue Jays’ booth after 30 seasons, and in 2024 baseball bid farewell to Bob Uecker (54 years with the Brewers), Joe Castiglione (42 years with the Red Sox) and, of course, the iconic John Sterling (36 years with the Yankees).

In fact, by my count —using Wikipedia’s team broadcaster pages — baseball has lost at least 16 TV/radio play-by-play or color commentators with 20+ years of service with a given team over the past decade, ranging from Rose and company this season to Vin Scully, who left the Dodgers in 2016 after 67 years as arguably THE voice of baseball, always and forever.

Those 15 names came from 15 different franchises, so among the four primary roles on baseball teams’ broadcasts — PBP or analyst, TV or radio — half of the league lost someone with multiple decades of institutional memory, if not far more.

That’s certainly true of Rose, who doubled as a Mets historian of sorts by virtue of not just his broadcasting tenure with the team, but also as someone who grew up going to games at Shea Stadium as a child. The power of having someone like that on the mic is the ability to connect present-day moments with those from decades earlier, weaving each new chapter into the larger tapestry of a team’s history.

In the lead-up to his final game, much was (rightly) made of the fact that Rose represented an unbroken lineage of radio commentators going back to the founding of the Mets before the 1962 season: At least one of Lindsey Nelson (who departed after the 1978 season), Bob Murphy (who left the radio booth in 2003) or Rose (who began calling games on TV in 1996 before moving to the radio in 2004) has been on the airwaves just about every night in franchise history.

The voices of the Mets

Like some other teams, the Mets have long used a distinctive setup on the radio with multiple “career broadcaster” types in the booth rather than a designated PBP announcer + an ex-player commentator type, as is almost always the model on TV — and during Rose’s radio era, he shared a booth with a number of names who would also be the PBP voice of other teams, including Tom McCarthy (Phillies), Wayne Hagin (Rockies), Josh Lewin (Rangers, Orioles, UCLA, San Diego Chargers),1 Wayne Randazzo (Angels) and Keith Raad (who could very well take over Rose’s spot in N.Y. next season). In that sense, Rose’s booth became something of a play-by-play nexus for the game of baseball, connecting voices that would eventually be heard across the sport’s broadcasting landscape.

And of course, that list also includes the great Gary Cohen, who has been either the Mets’ radio or TV voice going back to 1989, sharing the radio booth with Rose in 2004-05 — and whose own most iconic stint (as the ringleader of the incomparable SNY television booth alongside Ron Darling and Keith Hernandez) came after trading mediums with Rose in the mid-2000s. Going back to at least the ‘90s, the Mets have been blessed with a number of all-time standouts on the mic between Gary Thorne,2 Howie Rose, Cohen/Darling/Hernandez, and so forth.

But while baseball will have a few less of those with the retirements of names like Rose, Rizzs, Krukow and Martinez, the game has survived waves of similar departures before. From 2003-2013, for instance, 12 different voices with 20+ years of tenure left their teams, including Murphy (42 years) and Ralph Kiner (52 years!) from the Mets alone:

An earlier generation of similar iconic departures

The beauty of baseball is that the voices who narrate it are meant to come and go: Each new generation of broadcasters inherits the stories of the last one, then adds to them in their own way. And at the same time, numerous franchise fixtures do still remain in place as living encyclopedias for their teams. Again consulting the Wiki data (and excluding Rose, etc.), I find that 17 different current broadcasters — Cohen among them, with even more Mets service time than Rose — are working on 30+ years of tenure in some capacity with their teams:

Plenty of iconic baseball voices still remain, though

At some point soon, those voices will also make their way into the annals of history, making room for the following generation behind them — similar to how Rose will give way to Raad or someone else.

But for a franchise like the Mets, it does represent something meaningful to bid farewell to an announcer like Rose — born in Brooklyn in 1954, making him older than the franchise itself, and a fan as long as the team has existed. (Raad, by comparison, was born in 1993 — meaning he wasn’t even alive when Bobby Bonilla signed his first Mets contract.)

For more than three decades, Rose helped bridge the gap between what was happening on the field and what had happened before, putting countless Mets wins “in the books” along the way. And now, that’s where his own run belongs, too.

Note (Sept. 21, 7:18 PM): An earlier version of the first chart was missing longtime Toronto Blue Jays play-by-play announcer Jerry Howarth (1981-2017).
